newsitem.title: CANADA: Red River floods vast parts of Canadian province.
newsitem.headline: Red River floods vast parts of Canadian province.

text.p: Hundreds of soldiers scrambled on Thursday to build a 15-mile (24-km) long, six-foot (1.8-meter) high dike to defend the southwest flank of Manitoba's capital from a huge lake created by the largest Red River flood in 145 years.
"We are sparing no effort to get the Brunkild dike constructed," Manitoba Natural Resources flood liaison engineer Larry Whitney said.
At least 300 sq miles (776.9 sq km) of south Manitoba was under water on Thursday and up to 800 sq miles (2,072 sq km) should be submerged when the Red crests, Whitney said.
Two boys and a man were presumed drowned so far this week in connection with the flood, police said.
Winnipeg's Red River Floodway -- a dike built in 1968 to protect Winnipeg's 630,000 residents from flooding -- was raised 4.5 feet (1.5 metres) to divert the flood waters.
Hundreds of Canadian troops under Operation Noah and more than three dozen earth moving machines began extending a dike west of the Floodway on Thursday that must be completed by Sunday.
Two thousand troops were deployed across south Manitoba.
"The possibility exists to end run the west dike of the Floodway into the La Salle River system, and we've met with the local governments there to advise them," Whitney said.
At risk are the towns of Sanford, La Salle and southwest Winnipeg where sandbags were being put down on the main eight lane road linking to a highway bound for the United States.
The La Salle River drains into the Red River upstream of the Floodway inlet.
The C$63.2 million ($45.4 million), 29-mile (47-km) long, 30-foot (9-metre) deep, crescent-shaped ditch should protect 99 percent of the city's 650,000 residents, Whitney said.

A Manitoba Health Ministry spokesman said a plan was drafted to evacuate 1,400 hospital patients within Winnipeg in addition to the evacuation of half of the 500 patients at St. Boniface Hospital, across the Red River from downtown Winnipeg.
More than 17,000 residents of the Red River Valley between the U.S. border and Winnipeg have been ordered out of their homes but only 1,936 had complied by late afternoon on Thursday.
